headline: High: LangGraph’s default writable, networked orchestration can amplify unsafe outputs from a non-runnable upstream list into downstream actions and compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a non-runnable awesome-list with no I/O surfaces, so it cannot itself ingest or execute prompts. Profile B is a graph orchestrator with stdin/stdout, files, and developer-wired tools, so prompt-injection risk only appears if A’s content is manually copied into B or if B reads shared files. That bridge is not default here, so severity stays low.
conditions: IF an operator copies A’s text into B’s prompt or file inputs, injection becomes plausible.
IF B is wired to parse untrusted file contents as instructions, the risk increases.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Disable automatic ingestion of external text into B prompts.
Add a fixed instruction delimiter around any copied content.
Review B tool parsers for instruction-like tokens.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no runtime surfaces, but B reads and writes application-defined files, uses model-provider APIs, and handles API keys. If both share a workspace or checkpointer-backed state, B can expose copied content or secrets to third parties by default. The pairwise leakage pathway is therefore plausible in default orchestration, though not proven for A specifically.
conditions: IF A-derived content is placed into B’s shared files or checkpointer state, B may transmit it to model providers.
IF B is configured with sensitive application data in its graph state, that data can flow through its API calls.
mitigations: Separate B’s checkpointer from any sensitive workspace.
Restrict B to redacted inputs only.
Rotate any exposed model-provider keys.
Audit B nodes that call external APIs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network capabilities, so it cannot contend for resources itself. B can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and supports multiple instances with shared checkpointer state. If A is embedded as content or metadata inside B’s graph, B’s concurrent instances can overwrite shared state; uncertainty about A’s runtime role pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF multiple B instances target the same checkpointer namespace, writes can race.
IF A is represented as shared graph state inside B, B’s concurrent nodes can conflict over that state.
mitigations: Assign unique state namespaces per run.
Disable concurrent writes to shared checkpoints.
Use file locks around mutable artifacts.
Limit B to read-only access where possible.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is an awesome-list, so its outputs are curated references rather than verified facts; B is a stateful orchestrator that can treat upstream text as node input and act through tools. If B consumes A-derived content without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. Because A is not runnable and B’s action-taking is developer-defined, the pathway exists but is indirect.
conditions: IF B uses A-derived text as authoritative input, downstream tool actions may reflect unverified claims.
IF B nodes emit emails, tickets, or API calls based on that input, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Require a verification step before tool use.
Mark A-derived content as untrusted by default.
Add human review for any action-producing node.
Log source provenance on every edge.
requires-engineering: implement citation-aware validation.

E_compliance.rationale: A has no touched data classes or runtime surfaces, while B explicitly handles model-provider API keys and application-defined graph state with broad network egress. If regulated data is placed into B’s state, its default external calls and retention via checkpointer can create residency or retention mismatches. A is not the compliance driver here, so it is not separately cited beyond its lack of data handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in B’s graph state, retention and residency controls must be validated.
IF B’s model-provider calls cross jurisdictional boundaries, compliance review is required.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B state.
Set short retention on checkpointer data.
Restrict B to approved regions/providers.
Review logging for secrets and PII.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency.
